Is a Sailing Trip Worth It? I Spent a Week Onboard with More Sailing in the Caribbean to Find Out

November 17, 2026November 17, 2026 | by Alyssa
Last updated on November 17, 2026

Sharing my honest review of a More Sailing Caribbean trip
—

Have you ever wondered what a travel blogger’s email inbox is like?

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 45:18
Instaread

Chances are, probably not, and that’s totally normal. (I certainly didn’t when I first started blogging about travel almost a decade ago!)

Allow me to pull back the curtain a little: it’s pretty boring.

The most exciting my email gets is when I receive a message from a reader sharing their excitement over a trip they just took, but mostly, it’s kind of a mess, cluttered with sale alerts, press releases, and oodles of scams.

The never-ending deluge of scam and spam emails is why I initially deleted an email with a too-good-to-be-true subject line about a Caribbean sailing trip in October.

Our week aboard More Sailing was generously hosted, but this post is not sponsored. This guide contains affiliate links and I may receive a small commission if you make a purchase after clicking one of these links (at no additional cost to you!). Thank you for your support—it enables me to run this site ad-free!

But then that “what if” voice in my head piped up, and I fished it out of the trash, scrutinizing the contents carefully.

Inside was a warm and friendly invitation from a company that, frankly, I’d never heard of before: More Sailing.

I went straight to Google and discovered that More Sailing is a Swedish sailing company with more than fifteen years of experience offering small-group sailing trips across Europe and the Caribbean. Okay, I thought, I’ll bite, and I sent a cautious reply.

As you can see, that kind email turned out to be very much not a scam, and Michael and I recently spent a glorious week sailing around the Caribbean with a group of fellow travel bloggers. Before this trip, I’d never imagined a sailing vacation was within my reach, and if you’ve ever felt like that too, I cannot wait to introduce you to More Sailing.

WHAT IS MORE SAILING? 

About More Sailing

More Sailing got its start in 2009 on the west coast of Sweden, and the origin story is a good one because it’s a travel story. The founder traveled to Croatia for a week of sailing with friends and family, and what started as a single week-long trip turned into seven as people came and went from the boat. Everyone loved it so much that a plan took shape to make sailing holidays accessible to people who don’t necessarily own a boat (let alone know their port from their starboard!). This once-small operation has since grown into an international sailing company with a fleet of around 60 boats.

—

What destinations does More Sailing cover?

Today, More Sailing offers sailing trips in Croatia, Greece, Italy, the Caribbean, and along Sweden’s west coast. Most trips last around a week, while the Caribbean sailings run approximately 12–13 days, depending on the departure date.

—

Who are these trips designed for?

More Sailing’s trips are designed for people who want to experience a sailing vacation without having to own a boat, know how to sail, or organize a traditional yacht charter. The signature hosted sailing holidays include a professional skipper and onboard host, who take care of the sailing and day-to-day logistics so guests can simply enjoy the experience. Flights, transfers, meals, and other essentials are included in many packages, and they also offer group sailing trips, ideal for families, friends, and even corporate retreats.

MORE SAILING IN THE CARIBBEAN

More Sailing’s Caribbean trips depart from the spice island of Grenada, typically sailing north to Carriacou before continuing to St. Vincent and the Grenadines. Why “typically?” Well, the captain adjusts the itinerary based on the weather and sailing conditions. We took an abbreviated six-day version of the typical 12–13-day journey, exploring Carriacou and the southern Grenadines, including stops at Mayreau, Union Island, and Petit Tabac. But longer itineraries may continue farther north to St. Vincent and the northern Grenadines. It’s all kind of a beautiful mystery!

AURA 51 CATAMARAN LAYOUT

Deck and common spaces

More Sailing uses a Fountaine Pajot Aura 51 catamaran for its Caribbean trips. Guests have access to multiple indoor and outdoor common spaces on the 51-foot catamaran, including the open air forward deck, the open upper deck, the indoor lounge and galley, and the covered aft cockpit, which has a large dining table.

—

Cabins and sleeping arrangements

There are six cabins in total, with two larger cabins at the front, two medium-sized cabins in the middle, and two smaller cabins at the rear. But size comes with a trade-off: the larger cabins are the noisiest, while the smallest cabins are the quietest.

Whichever you choose, expect snug quarters. The bed takes up most of the room (and is slightly narrower at one end), with just a little storage space for your belongings. Each cabin also has a private bathroom with a toilet, sink, and shower. Both the bedroom and bathroom have skylights that you can open for extra airflow, plus there’s a fan in the bedroom for when the air conditioning isn’t running. You’ll also find one 230V outlet and a few USB charging ports for your devices.

It really is just the essentials, but that’s okay. The cabin isn’t where you want to linger on this kind of trip anyway.

—

Bathrooms and showers

The in-cabin private bathrooms are surprisingly spacious for a boat, although there’s not quite enough room for two people to brush their teeth at the same time. There’s a small cabinet under the sink, a shelf beneath the mirror, and a few hooks on the walls for toiletries, towels, and other odds and ends.

One thing worth knowing before you set sail is that the toilets are marine toilets, which operate a little differently from the ones at home. Don’t worry, though—the crew will give you a demonstration before departure so you’ll know exactly what to do. Additionally, the captain and host do not have their own bathroom, so they may ask to borrow yours during the trip (however, you can say no if you’re not comfortable—as long as one or two cabins say yes, at least).

WHAT DAILY LIFE ONBOARD IS REALLY LIKE

A typical day from morning to night

The reality of this kind of trip is that no two days are ever exactly the same—but there is a certain rhythm to days on a More Sailing catamaran. Mornings begin when you decide they do, although breakfast is served at a set time each day (8 a.m. on our sailing). The captain holds a morning meeting to share the day’s route, and depending on the plan, you may have time for a swim before departure or you may be setting sail shortly after.

Within the next hour or so, you’ll anchor in another splendid location, where you’ll have the chance to swim or perhaps take the dinghy over to shore for a little beach time. Once the sun (and your hunger) peaks, your host will set out a family-style lunch to enjoy together. You may linger after lunch, or you might depart right away for your final stop of the day, heading up to the top deck to soak in the views along the way. Once you arrive, you might decide to stay on board and read for a bit, or grab your mask and snorkel and hop back in the water. It’s totally up to you.

As the sun sets, the beer and wine come out, and after getting ready for dinner, you can relax and enjoy happy hour with your fellow passengers. When it’s time to head ashore for dinner, you’ll climb back into the dinghy in groups (which you might find more difficult after a glass or two!)

You’ll climb out of the dinghy onto the beach, where you’ll likely find an outdoor table softly illuminated by twinkling lights and plates piled high with local favorites like rice, plantains, fish, spiny lobster, and more. You might be talked into an overproof rum punch, but that’s just how things are when you’re on vacation in the Caribbean.

Tumbling back into the dinghy, you’ll head back to the catamaran, where you might keep toasting the night away over great conversation or perhaps head up to the top deck for some stargazing. When you decide to turn in for the night, simply head downstairs to your cabin and climb into bed so you can do it all over again, but entirely differently, tomorrow.

—

The food and drinks onboard

While guests enjoy dinner ashore each night, the onboard host prepares breakfast and lunch in the tiny galley. It was such a treat to wake up each morning to a hearty spread of cheeses, meats, yogurt, fresh fruit, eggs, juices, and even homemade bread prepared by Ronja. Lunch was a different home-cooked meal each day, served family-style, and I always looked forward to seeing what Ronja had cooked up for us as we gathered around the table. And just when I started craving something sweet, an afternoon snack would appear, whether it was cookies, warm banana bread, or an apple tart, all served with coffee.

Water and soft drinks (including banana Fanta—you have to try it!) are available all day from the self-serve fridge, and beer and wine are available after 11 a.m. The website indicates that beer and wine are available in limited quantities, but our group never hit that limit. (Rumor has it that some other groups in the past have!)

—

Your fellow passengers

Our group included fellow travel bloggers and their companions, and while none of us knew one another going in, we all left as friends. On a More Sailing trip, you could find yourself sharing the boat with travelers of just about any age, which I think adds to the fun. Worried about being in such close proximity to strangers? Don’t be. I found that this kind of trip tends to attract people who are just as interested in meeting fellow travelers as they are in seeing somewhere new.

—

Swimming, snorkeling, and time on the water

That blue, blue water is so tempting on a hot Caribbean day—and thankfully, you’ll have plenty of opportunities to enjoy it. The captain will open the guard ropes on the back of the boat whenever it’s clear to swim, and you can jump in and climb out as you’d like. In addition to swimming, the clear water also makes for some excellent snorkeling. Be sure to pack your mask and snorkel (and fins if you’d like)!

Not a strong swimmer? That’s okay! You don’t need to get in the water if you’re not comfortable. But if you do decide to dip your toe in, you can grab a life jacket at any time for added reassurance. You can also take the dinghy ashore at certain stops and wade into the shallow waters without going deeper than your comfort level.

—

Wi-Fi, charging, and staying connected

It’s easy to assume you’ll have Wi-Fi just about everywhere these days, but believe it or not, there’s no Wi-Fi aboard a More Sailing catamaran That said, Michael and I both had cell service for all but five minutes of our trip, and we never worried about feeling completely disconnected.

To charge your devices, each cabin has one 230V Type F outlet and several USB-A ports, though these may not always be available when the generator isn’t running, so plan to pack a portable charger just in case (solar is a smart idea!).

—

Privacy and downtime

A trip like this is fairly social by nature, but that doesn’t mean you won’t have opportunities to escape for some downtime. You can always head to your cabin, of course, but I often found there were quiet spots on the upper and forward decks throughout the day. Even when someone else was on the same deck, I found it was easy to enjoy some peace and quiet without feeling like we were constantly on top of one another.

MY MORE SAILING CARIBBEAN EXPERIENCE

I should preface this by saying my sailing experience was a little different from most. All of the guests on our sailing were fellow travel bloggers and their companions, and our trip was shorter than a typical More Sailing Caribbean itinerary. But then again, no two More Sailing trips are really ever the same…

My Week Onboard

We never really know what to expect when visiting a new place, but we usually have other destinations or similar experiences to draw on to help us know what to expect. With a weeklong sailing trip on the horizon, I had no such reference point. It was all uncharted territory.

At least I knew how to get us to Grenada, and I booked a flight that landed on the island the day before we were scheduled to embark. This gave us some breathing room in case our flight was delayed (or worse, canceled), while also giving us a chance to explore a bit of Grenada and get a good night’s sleep after our 3 a.m. airport wake-up call.

By the time our first sailing day arrived, we’d already exchanged a few messages with Captain Morgan and host Ronja in a WhatsApp group chat, and we were feeling a bit more prepared for the journey. We hailed a ride to the marina shortly before 6 p.m., and soon after arriving, we spotted some of our fellow guests. A moment later, Ronja found us and led us to our catamaran, the Ingrid.

Even though we had arrived at the marina a few minutes early, we were the last ones to board the boat. That could have been an awkward entrance, but everyone slipped right into easy conversation, comparing notes about our time in Grenada so far. After a short safety briefing, a rundown of the onboard rules, and the unfortunate news that our watermaker was broken and the replacement part hadn’t arrived in time so we’d need to refill the tank periodically, we collectively had to pick out which cabins we’d call home for the rest of the journey.

We didn’t have a preference, so we wound up in one of the middle cabins (if this was a Goldilocks and the Three Bears situation, our cabin would have belonged to Mama Bear) and deposited our belongings. Normally, we’d unpack for a stay this long, but we quickly decided it would be easier to leave everything in our bags and set them on the storage cabinet at the end of the bed. Back upstairs we went, where Ronja had set out a snacky first-night feast of nachos, charcuterie, garlic bread, chips, and more. We all filled our plates and found a place to sit, getting to know one another and discovering some mutual connections we already shared.

By then, we’d made our first short sail and anchored not far from the marina. As we chatted, a sense of cold dread began to settle over me. The boat had begun rocking back and forth in the dark, and with only the lights of nearby boats bobbing on the water to focus on, seasickness washed over me. It hit fast and it hit hard, and in a panic, I sent Michael down to the cabin to fetch the medication while I excused myself and headed to the upper deck for some fresh air. Have I made a huge mistake? I wondered to myself over and over, calculating what it might cost to return to the marina and book a last-minute hotel for six nights.

I don’t know how long I stayed up there—probably an hour or two—but eventually, I felt steady enough to rejoin the rest of the passengers. It’s never fun to miss out on the early moments of getting to know a group, but everyone was so kind and understanding. I’ll admit the rest of the evening is a bit hazy, as my brain was preoccupied with trying to make sense of the motion around me (and the double dose of medication was kicking in), but I know I took a short shower and headed to bed early to try to sleep off the icky feeling.

By the time I awoke the next morning, I felt like a new person. I’m not sure if it was the medicine, the sunshine, the sleep, or having the horizon in plain view, but I chided myself for considering leaving. I was ready and raring to go for whatever adventures lay ahead (though I knew better than to tempt fate, so I kept taking the motion sickness medication and stashed my phone away to avoid looking at it). But when I looked around at breakfast and saw only a few of my fellow passengers seated across from me, I realized that although my seasickness had passed, it had struck others overnight.

Eventually, everyone made their way up to the deck, and Captain Morgan led the first of the week’s morning meetings. Over breakfast each morning, he’d pull out a nautical map of Grenada and St. Vincent and the Grenadines to show us the planned route based on the weather and wind conditions.

Our first day included the longest and roughest stretch of sailing of the entire trip, apart from the return journey. After breakfast, I made a beeline for a shady spot on the top deck so the horizon would always be in view. I assumed a catamaran would glide quite smoothly with its two hulls, but we encountered a few surprisingly choppy stretches that left us holding on to our seats.

As we approached land, the water grew calmer and took on the most brilliant turquoise hue as we pulled into the bay at Carriacou a little after noon. While we tucked into big bowls of spicy noodles for lunch, the captain collected our passports and took them ashore so we could officially clear out of Grenada and continue into the Grenadines.

After lunch, we made the short crossing to postcard-perfect Sandy Island, where we grabbed our masks and snorkels to explore the reef along the shoreline. Watching colorful fish dart between hiding spots (though a few brave and curious ones came to investigate us, too!) was such a treat.

We spent a couple of hours on the island before it was time to head to dinner. From then on, we’d hop in the dinghy each evening and head to a different beach restaurant for dinner—some with modern amenities, while others were much more rustic, with limited menus that required us to order in advance. Not all of them accepted credit cards, so we were glad we’d taken out cash in Grenada before setting sail.

When we returned to the catamaran after dinner on our first full day, we were dismayed to find that we were entirely out of fresh water for bathing, flushing, or washing dishes (though we still had more than a week’s supply of bottled drinking water onboard, not to mention wine, beer, and soda). Captain Morgan shared his plan to refill the water tank on a nearby island the following morning, and provided us each with bottles of seawater for flushing our cabin toilets. I would have loved nothing more than a hot shower after spending the day swimming in salt water, but that wasn’t possible—luckily, I’d packed a few shower wipes at the last minute, so I ripped one in half for Michael and me to use. After brushing our teeth with bottled water, we tumbled into bed, too exhausted to care that we were still a bit salty.

Now, I would love to give you a day-by-day recap of the rest of our time on board, but then this post would take a gazillion hours to read. The good news? Each day followed a similar rhythm, just in a different location. We did manage to refill the water tank the following day, and several more times throughout the trip, as it never seemed to last long. We were asked to bathe in the sea off the back of the boat, so we’d soap up while wearing our swimsuits and then give ourselves a quick freshwater rinse with the hose.

I admit, I was kind of uncomfortable at the thought of going so long without a traditional shower, but at the same time, what can you do? Within a day or two, we had our makeshift shower routine down pat (though I’ll confess to snagging an extra drinking bottle for a more thorough rinse in the cabin).

The days glided by, much like our catamaran, as we sailed from Carriacou into the southern Grenadines. Each day, we pulled into yet another beautiful bay, snorkeled with sea life (including sea turtles, for the first time in my life!), enjoyed fresh meals, and wound down the evening with our toes in the sand, raising a glass to the day. It didn’t take long for us to lose track of the days, and it felt as if we’d simultaneously been sailing for months and for mere moments.

All too soon, we returned to the marina in Grenada for our final night, enjoying a positively epic sunset that felt like a fitting send-off, an admittedly forgettable meal at a nearby restaurant, and an unbelievably wonderful shower. The following morning, we all shared one final breakfast and bid farewell to Morgan and Ronja. Some of our group stayed on to explore more of Grenada, and the rest of us headed for the airport. I can’t speak for everyone, but I think this is a trip that will stick with all of us for a long time.

—

What I Loved and What I Would Change

I went into this trip not really knowing what to expect, and that turned out to be a wonderful thing. Travel planning usually falls to me, and I was a little worried about giving up my usual role of leading our trips. But you know what? Not having to make 35,000 decisions in a day felt absolutely amazing, and I quickly learned to go with the flow.

Spending so much time admiring the scenery was good for the nervous system, but swimming in that gorgeous water and coming face-to-face with more sea life than I’d ever seen outside an aquarium was good for the soul. I haven’t swum so much in years, and my body enjoyed the gentle exercise.

Perhaps my favorite surprise came at mealtimes. Never in a million years would I have thought we’d be enjoying homemade bread straight from the oven or such fresh produce at sea, and yet, Ronja always managed to create an impressive spread from the teeny tiny galley.

But even the dreamiest vacation takes place in real life, so there were a few things I would have changed if given the chance. The first, of course, was our broken watermaker. The crew did an amazing job of arranging refills for us every day or so, which isn’t an easy feat in the Caribbean, but I definitely missed having a proper shower at the end of the day. (The good news is that the replacement parts have since been delivered, so the watermaker should be back up and running for future trips.)

We also spent very little time exploring the towns ashore, which was a bit of a surprise to all of us. On the one occasion we went ashore while the water tank was being refilled, we found that most businesses on the island were closed because it was still low season. Given the length of our trip and the islands we visited, I’m not sure how many opportunities we actually missed, but I would have liked a little more time on land to break up the days.

Lastly, while I’m incredibly proud of myself for keeping up with a tedious sunscreen regimen, I still wound up with a few small patches of sunburn. There was always plenty of shade in the galley and aft cockpit, but the upper deck had no permanent shade. Unless you were seated under the sail at just the right angle, you were fully exposed to the sun while up there. It would have been nice to have some kind of retractable shade option (though I’m sure it’s both expensive to install and tedious to deal with).

Even with a few hiccups along the way, I came away from this trip with a whole new appreciation for sailing and the magic that happens on a small group trip.

WHAT TO PACK FOR A MORE SAILING CARIBBEAN TRIP

I’ve never felt more out of my element packing for a vacation than I did preparing for a weeklong sailing trip. If you’ve been reading for a while, you might be familiar with my series of packing guides, most of which are for city destinations (with the occasional outdoorsy-themed trip in the mix). Packing for a catamaran is a different ballgame from packing for those trips, starting with the bag itself

More Sailing recommends bringing a soft-sided bag rather than a rolling hard-shell suitcase (my go-to). Michael and I already each had a carry-on-size duffle on hand (a canvas weekender for him, and a garment duffle for me). They worked great on the boat, but navigating the airport with a heavy bag grew old even before our first layover. If I had to do it all over again, I’d choose a rolling duffle instead. Still soft and easy to stash away on board, but much gentler on the back.

As for what goes inside the bag, you’ll want to focus more on function rather than looks. Swimsuits are a non-negotiable (I reached for my Left on Friday suits more than any others), and at least two cover-ups would be a wise move. Clothes dry pretty quickly on the boat’s lines when it’s sunny, but if it rains, you may have to hang them up in your cabin to dry. You should pack a beach towel as well, as your fare only includes one bath towel per person. I don’t often recommend shopping before a trip, but trust that you’ll be grateful if you pack a Turkish towel (if you don’t already have one) instead of a terry towel. I’d also recommend packing darker clothing, as some of the boat’s drying lines had rusty spots.

But what about your regular clothes? Well, I wouldn’t waste precious luggage space on anything, well, too precious. I packed two dresses and two skirts with plans to wear them to dinner throughout the week, but ended up wearing just one of them, and only once. Instead, you should plan to keep things casual, and expect to get a little wet as you climb in and out of the dinghy. Quick-drying shorts with an elastic waist are your friend here (I’m obsessed with these shorts with zippered pockets, and I’m not even exaggerating). Pair them with easy tanks and tees, and you’re set. A lightweight shell rain jacket is also a good idea in case of showers.

I trust you know what underwear and pajamas to pack, but you probably need fewer pairs of shoes than you think. The pre-trip notes indicated that we could wear white-soled shoes on board, but at our safety briefing, we were instructed to go barefoot while on the boat to keep it clean. I noticed that I felt safer going barefoot anyway when the deck was slippery, but I’d still pack a pair of waterproof light-soled or white-soled sandals for the evenings, though.

Okay, so that’s all the clothing covered, but there are still more essentials I recommend packing for your sailing trip. Note that if you’re not checking a bag, you may want to purchase a few of these items after you arrive (especially sunscreen). It’s a lot, so let’s go straight into list mode:

  • Sunscreen for face and body
  • Aloe
  • Bug spray
  • Seasickness medications, bands, and patches
  • Pain relievers, anti-diarrheal medication, and any regular medications.
  • First-aid kit
  • Shampoo, conditioner, and body wash (these are not included in your cabin)
  • Waterless shaving stick
  • Shower wipes
  • Face wipes
  • Anti-chafe stick
  • Waterproof mascara and remover (don’t forget the second part!)
  • Mini fan
  • International adapter (Grenada uses a Type G plug and the catamaran uses a Type F), plus a voltage converter if you need it
  • Solar charger for when the generator is not running
  • Action camera for capturing underwater adventures
  • Waterproof phone pouch
  • Snorkel and mask (and fins, if you’d like)
  • All the other hygiene goodies you usually pack (toothbrush, toothpaste, floss, razor, deodorant, etc.)

Shop my catamaran sailing essentials:

What’s missing? Well, a few things that I would consider essentials on any other trip. I waffled over whether to bring any hair tools (hair dryer, curling iron), and I’m so glad I didn’t. For one, I’m not sure the catamaran could have powered them. For another, it was kind of nice to just embrace my air-dried hair (though I did bring along some styling cream to help things along). I also kept my makeup to an absolute minimum, wearing just my mascara, a tinted lip balm, and glowy sunscreen for the week.

On the tech front, I debated bringing my MacBook, then decided to leave it at home. I’m glad I did. Even though my seasickness passed quickly, I think it would have reared its head again had I pulled out a screen. Just using my phone for a few minutes was enough to make the queasy feeling start to creep back in.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ABOUT MORE SAILING

I don’t know that my Instagram inbox has ever been this full during a trip before! I’ll try to answer your most common questions here:

Do I need sailing experience?

Good news for all of us landlubbers: no sailing experience is needed. But if you’ve ever been curious about sailing, your captain will be more than happy to show you the ropes and let you try your hand at it.

That said, you do need to have a certain level of mobility to navigate life at sea. Some of the challenges include transferring between the boat and the dinghy, moving through tight spaces, and keeping your balance on slippery, moving decks.

How much does a More Sailing Caribbean trip cost?

It varies greatly depending on the dates you choose, but I would say most 12-day Caribbean sailings cost around $5,000 USD per person. Winter holiday weeks naturally bring that number up, but as of the time of writing, I’ve seen at least one sailing priced around $3,700 USD per person.

Flexible? I’ve spotted some last-minute discounts on their site before, so that’s worth checking out too.

What is included in the price?

A More Sailing trip is almost a prepaid all-inclusive vacation, and your trip costs cover: your skipper and host, breakfast, lunch, and snacks, drinks on-board (soft drinks, wine, and beer), all marina fees, and linens in your cabin. For guests traveling from Sweden, airfare and ground transfers are also included. Guests traveling from elsewhere receive a $1,000 USD discount instead, but are responsible for arranging their own flights and transportation. It does not include dinners ashore, souvenirs or additional purchases, or gratuities.

Do I need to bring cash?

Yes, as there are many places in Grenada and the Grenadines that only accept cash. The local currency here is the Eastern Caribbean Dollar (EC), and I’d recommend withdrawing cash at the airport if possible, followed by a bank or the marina. Local ATMs can sometimes run out of cash, so it’s best not to leave it until the last minute. More Sailing recommends budgeting EC$150 (approximately US$55.50) per person per day, and I’d say that’s a pretty good estimate. We came in a little under that recommendation most days, but not so much that I’d recommend taking out less cash.

Will I get seasick?

While I can’t say for certain, in this case, seasickness is one of those things where it’s best to prepare for the worst and hope for the best. You’ll want to stay hydrated, always have some food in your belly, get some fresh air, keep your eyes on the horizon, and pack an arsenal of medications and remedies. It might be tempting to scroll on your phone to distract yourself, but that’ll only make things worse. (But if you do need to use your phone throughout your trip, make sure you enable Vehicle Motion Cues on your iPhone or Motion Assist on your Android phone.)

I got over my seasickness within about twelve hours, but what I didn’t anticipate was feeling seasick on land after returning. It took both Michael and me three or four solid days to get our land legs back after disembarking, and those days were largely spent feeling icky on the sofa and going for the occasional walk or drive to give our brains a little motion relief. After all our efforts Googling our symptoms, I learned that there’s no universally effective treatment for Mal de Débarquement syndrome (MdDS), although symptoms often resolve on their own. For some people, they can linger much longer. If you’re able, give yourself plenty of time to get back on your feet after your trip. If I could do it again, I don’t know if I’d fly home the same day that we docked.

How many people are onboard?

For the Caribbean sailings, there are typically up to fourteen people on board: twelve guests across six cabins, plus the captain and host.

Will I have to share a cabin?

No, you can request a single cabin by contacting More Sailing’s sales team at boka@moresailing.se. Note that the fares posted on the website are per person with double occupancy, so a person booking a single cabin should expect to pay more.

What is the food like?

Based on my experience, the meals varied from day to day, although some familiar favorites made appearances throughout the trip. Breakfast usually included a buffet of savory and sweet options, with a mix of eggs, fresh fruit, sliced meats and cheeses, yogurts, and granola (some days we were even treated to fresh rolls, still steaming hot from the oven!). I’m not usually a big breakfast person, but I always made an exception for a hearty start to the day on the catamaran. The one downside? Instant coffee. But I completely understand the convenience of it, of course.

Lunch was another highlight, with a mix of hot and cold elements served family-style (so refreshing at the hottest part of the day!). We enjoyed taco bowls, chicken Caesar wraps, rice noodles, and more, all surprisingly fresh considering we were cooking and eating at sea. Dinner was usually a beach barbecue, with a different restaurant or beachside spot each night (paid separately). The setting varied from full-service outdoor restaurants to humble huts, but more often than not, menus typically offered a choice of chicken, fish, lobster, or ribs, served alongside rice, plantains, and vegetables.

Can they accommodate dietary restrictions?

Yes! Your host will be happy to accommodate your dietary restrictions, as long as you let them know in advance.

Is there Wi-Fi onboard?

No, there’s no WiFi on the catamaran, which is the perfect excuse to disconnect and enjoy the scenery. That said, you may still have cell service depending on your carrier and where you’re sailing. If you truly need to stay connected, I recommend checking with your mobile carrier for international plan options or purchasing an eSIM. I went with OneRoam’s 7-Day Unlimited land-only plan, and was surprised to find I had excellent cell service for nearly the entire trip, with just one brief stretch without service, even though we were on the water for a week straight. Save 15% on your eSIM with the OneRoam promo code WAYWARD15.

Are the showers and bathrooms the same as back home?

While I’m pretty sure I’ve never taken a shower at your house to confirm or deny, I can say that unless you live on a sailboat, the bathrooms on board the catamaran are ever so slightly different from bathrooms on dry land. First of all, they’re pretty compact spaces, with room for only one person at a time (i.e., you’ll need to take turns brushing your teeth!). And each element felt slightly more compact than I’m used to. The sink and shower were smaller, and maybe I’m just imagining it, but I think even the toilet was, too.

But the good news is that each of those elements operates pretty intuitively, with the exception of the toilet. To flush, you’ll need to press one button to fill the tank with water, then a second button to open the hatch and let gravity do its job. Just be sure to never flush paper or other items down; there’s a wastebasket that gets emptied daily for that.

Is alcohol included in a More Sailing trip?

Wine and beer are included on all More Sailing trips except on their sailings in Sweden. If your brain immediately jumped to “booze cruise,” I completely understand, but I can honestly say that ours was not at all like that. Alcohol is unavailable until after 11 a.m., and I got the impression that the captain would be quick to put a stop to any foolishness. Instead, people simply grabbed a beer or glass of wine to enjoy with lunch or up on the deck. It’s a vacation, after all, and no one had anywhere to drive.

Is it safe?

That’s a loaded question—one I’d never be able to answer for you about any destination (even your hometown!). But I will say this: I felt safe throughout my week with More Sailing. The crew ran a safety briefing on day one, showed us where the life jackets and first aid kit were kept, and were always ready to adjust the itinerary based on the weather conditions. As with any boat trip, watch your footing on deck, wear a life jacket when instructed, and put one on whenever you’d feel more comfortable doing so. It’s certainly not a bad idea to check with your credit card provider to see what type of travel insurance might be included (this is my favorite travel credit card for its approachable annual fee and included travel benefits) or add on a separate travel insurance policy for peace of mind.

When is the best time of year to go?

The More Sailing Caribbean route is seasonal, typically starting in late October/early November and running through the end of April. Hands down, the best time to sail in this part of the Caribbean is during the dry season, which typically runs from January through April. That said, temperatures remain fairly constant year-round, and our October trip only saw a handful of showers that were gone in a blink. My recommendation: take a spring or late winter trip if you can swing it, but don’t skip it if you can only travel in the fall.

How do I get to the departure port?

Airfare and transfers are included for guests traveling from Sweden, making it easy to get from home to the departure port. As for the rest of us? We have to make our own way to Grenada. There are direct flights to Maurice Bishop International Airport from several major U.S. cities, including New York, Miami, Atlanta, and Charlotte, and many others that only require one connection.

From the airport, you can either arrange private transportation, jump in a taxi, or use the local take on Uber, Haylup (that’s my referral link for a little bonus!). We found that choosing the smallest car often meant a longer wait, but paying a little extra for a standard ride sped things up. Some drivers may even offer their contact information so you can book directly next time, if you’re comfortable doing so.

Where do I stay if I want to spend more time in Grenada?

Grenada has a wide range of accommodation options, from short-term rentals to five-star luxury resorts. I was surprised to find that many hotels and resorts close for October in Grenada, but I managed to find a great value with our stay at Blue Horizons Garden Resort. The grounds here were stunning, and our room was spacious and comfortable, though some might find it dated. Breakfast at La Belle Creole was fresh and delicious (don’t miss the nutmeg pancakes!), and the poolside bar’s lunch menu looked delightful, too. But this hotel is also ideal from a location standpoint—it’s about halfway between the airport and the marina, and just a five-minute walk from Grand Anse Beach as well as a local mall with a bank and grocery store for last-minute essentials.

Is a sailboat trip better than a resort vacation or a cruise?

The answer to this question will vary wildly from person to person, but I think it all boils down to what you’re looking for in a trip. Someone who just wants to park their bum in one pretty place (any pretty place!) might find the constant moving around of a sailing trip unnecessary, and would probably be happier at an all-inclusive resort. Someone who wants to sample a few different destinations while enjoying scheduled activities and plenty of dining options might prefer a traditional cruise. And someone who’d rather get to know one destination in greater depth is probably better off flying in and spending a few days exploring on their own (or adding some time before or after a sailing!).

In my humble opinion, a sailing trip combines some of the best parts of all three into one pretty memorable vacation.

MY FINAL VERDICT: IS A MORE SAILING CARIBBEAN TRIP REALLY WORTH IT?

I went into this trip with very little idea of what to expect, and I came away fully understanding why people fall in love with sailing vacations. Some of the tiny bays we visited are places a cruise ship could never reach, and we never would have seen them all if we’d simply plopped ourselves at one resort for the weekend. But sailing isn’t just a way to get from one place to another. Time spent on the boat itself is part of the experience, and I found I especially loved the slower pace and the fact that my only decisions tended to be things like, “Do I want to swim or not?” and “Should I head to the upper deck for some quiet time or join the others for a spirited conversation?” and “Would I like a beer or a glass of wine?”

Of course, life on a catamaran isn’t without its quirks. You do have limited personal space, a little less control over how long you spend at a destination, and the occasional reminder that you’re living on a boat (never clearer to me than when we ran out of fresh water!). And while I loved getting to explore a new stretch of coastline each day, the local culture of the Grenadines is still a bit of a mystery to me.

But if you love being on the water, enjoy a little adventure, and are cool with a bit of “roughing it” in order to reach sparkling turquoise bays, I think you’ll have a wonderful time. I certainly came away with a new appreciation for sailing, and I’d happily do it again in a heartbeat. In fact, I’m already eyeing those eight-day sailings in Greece…

—

Questions for you

Have you ever taken a sailing vacation?

What’s one place you’ve visited that you think would be even better explored by boat?

If you could book a sailing trip anywhere in the world, where would you go?
